title: The Listening Portrait
premise: Felix Galloway returns to the decaying family house to bury their twin, Wren, only to find that Wren's body was never quite empty. The house has been singing a lullaby their mother taught them as children, and every mirror in it now reflects a heartbeat behind reality—showing Felix what they were too afraid to see: that staying invisible let something else take up residence in their absence. As neighbors who once ignored Felix begin hearing the song too, drawn toward the house like moths, Felix realizes the entity wearing Wren's face needs a living voice to finish the lullaby's last verse and fully cross over. In the end, Felix refuses to sing alone but finds strength in an unlikely found family of fellow 'listeners' the song has marked over generations; together they sing the verse wrong on purpose, breaking the melody's power, though Felix must bury their twin a second time—and this time mean goodbye.
about_author: Freya Galloway is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing estate sales in coastal New England, where she developed a lasting unease about inherited houses. She writes horror about families that keep things in the walls, and about the quiet people who finally stop being quiet.

chapters.title: The Wrong Sibling
chapters.summary: Felix arrives at the Galloway house for Wren's funeral, numb with seven years of avoidance. POV: Felix. Sorting Wren's room, they find sheet music annotated in handwriting that keeps changing. The emotional beat is guilt sharpening into dread when Felix hums a bar of the lullaby and hears it hummed back from inside the walls.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: POV: Felix. The morning after the funeral, every mirror reflects the room a beat behind. Felix tests them obsessively, telling themselves it's grief, exhaustion, anything. A neighbor, Mrs. Okonkwo, mentions she heard singing all night. Emotional beat: the fragile comfort of rational explanation cracking under repetition.

chapters.title: What Mother Taught Us
chapters.summary: POV: Felix, with flashbacks to childhood. Felix uncovers their mother's journals revealing the lullaby was never a lullaby—it's a summons, taught to twins so one could always answer. The house's previous owners all had twins. All lost one. Emotional beat: the sick recognition that Felix's invisibility was protection someone paid for.

chapters.title: Wren, Mostly
chapters.summary: POV: Felix. Something wearing Wren's mannerisms appears at dusk—not hostile, almost tender, asking Felix to help it remember the last verse. It knows childhood secrets no ghost should. Emotional beat: longing warring with terror; Felix wants their twin back so badly they nearly sing along before catching themselves.

chapters.title: The Listeners
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Mrs. Okonkwo. She reveals she grew up two streets away and has heard the song her whole life; her brother answered it in 1974. She introduces Felix to three other survivors the song has marked—a retired choir director, a teenage boy, a mute fisherman. Emotional beat: the first warmth of found family, people who believe without proof.

chapters.title: Verse by Verse
chapters.summary: POV: Felix. The group maps the lullaby's structure using the mother's journals and the choir director's ear: each verse sung correctly lets the entity take more shape; the last verse completes it. The mirrors now show rooms that don't exist, furnished with the missing listeners' lives. Emotional beat: dread becoming resolve—they will learn the song to unmake it.

chapters.title: Invisible No More
chapters.summary: POV: the entity, briefly, then Felix. The thing in Wren's skin stops pretending, showing Felix how power works here: whoever finishes the song commands the house and everyone in it. It offers Felix belonging, importance, an end to smallness. Emotional beat: temptation at its most seductive—the corruption of power dressed as love.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Answered
chapters.summary: POV: the teenager, Dev. Drawn by dreams, Dev sings two lines alone and begins fading from mirrors, his voice joining the house's chorus. The group races to pull him back, and the fisherman gives his own voice—permanently—to anchor him. Emotional beat: sacrifice proving this makeshift family is real, and that the cost is climbing.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: POV: Felix. On the anniversary of the twins' birth, the house pulls all its listeners in. The entity, nearly whole, sings the final verse and demands Felix harmonize. Instead, Felix sings it deliberately wrong—flat, broken, human—and the others join, each mangling it differently until the melody collapses. Emotional beat: defiant imperfection as salvation; the climax shatters the mirrors mid-reflection.

chapters.title: A Second Burial
chapters.summary: POV: Felix, weeks later. The house is silent; the mirrors are honest again. Felix buries what remains of Wren properly, grieving the real twin at last, and chooses to stay—not hiding, but keeping watch, teaching the surviving listeners the song only so they'll know which notes never to sing. Emotional beat: belonging chosen freely, grief carried openly, quiet peace earned.
